Mahjong: Game-Night Refresher

For players who have played before but need the whole game put back together quickly. Based on your photographed hand sheets and tile set.

60-second memory reset

Your basic job: keep improving your hand until it matches a legal Mahjong pattern. On an ordinary turn, draw one tile, then discard one tile. Watch every discard because you may be able to claim it.
345 = Chow   777 = Pung   NNNN = Kong

Chow = sequencePung = 3 alikeKong = 4 alikePair = 2 alike

Important for your group: your sheets use Fishing as a real game state. An asterisk (*) beside a special hand means that once you are Fishing, you may take the last required tile from the centre/discards. A double asterisk (**) means you cannot pick up at all; the required tiles must come from the wall. No asterisk means the centre may be used to complete a Pung/Kong/Chow as permitted by the hand.

1. Set up & deal

Mix the tiles face down thoroughly and build the walls in the way your group normally uses.
Choose/confirm East (dealer) and the other seat winds. Keep the prevailing/round wind marker if your group uses one.
Deal the starting hands. East begins with the extra tile needed to make the first discard; everyone else starts ready to draw.
Sort privately. Group by suit, then Winds/Dragons. Immediately look for pairs, connected numbers and obvious special-hand possibilities.
House-rule checkpoint: your uploaded material is primarily the special-hand reference, not the original setup/scoring rule pages. If your group has a remembered convention for wall break, exact deal, Flowers/Seasons, or dealer rotation, use that convention tonight rather than replacing it with another Mahjong variant.

Know what you're looking at

Your own photograph is the fastest visual reminder. The three numbered suits are Characters, Bamboos, and Circles/Dots. The honours are Winds (E/S/W/N) and Dragons.

2. The rhythm of every turn

Draw. Take the next tile from the wall unless your turn arose from a legal claim.
Reassess. Did the tile complete a set, improve a run, make a useful pair, or move you toward a named hand?
Declare anything required (for example a Kong) before continuing, using your group's normal procedure.
Discard one tile face up. Say it clearly. Once discarded, everyone should have a chance to react before play moves on.

Beginner strategy: early in the hand, keep flexible connected tiles such as 3-4, 4-6, or pairs. Isolated tiles—especially ones that do not fit your developing hand—are natural discard candidates. But a named special hand can completely change that advice.

3. When somebody discards a tile

You need it for…What it means
ChowIt completes a three-number sequence in one suit.
PungYou already hold two identical tiles; the discard gives you three.
KongIt completes four identical tiles, subject to the rules of the hand you are pursuing.
Mahjong / final tileIt completes your legal winning hand; special-hand restrictions still matter.
After a successful claim: expose the completed set if required by your rules, then discard so play can continue. A Kong normally requires the group's usual replacement-tile procedure.

Do not automatically grab a discard just because it fits. Exposing a set can destroy a concealed-hand bonus or make a special hand illegal. Check the hand you are pursuing first.

4. Fishing — the point everyone forgets

Think of Fishing as: “My hand is complete except for the final required tile.” At that point, the special-hand sheet tells you how that last tile may be obtained.

Mark on your sheetPractical meaning
*Once Fishing, you may pick up the last tile from the centre/discards.
**You cannot pick up at all; all required tiles must be drawn from the wall.
No *The sheet says you may pick up from the centre to make a Pung/Kong/Chow.
Table habit: when you reach Fishing, say it clearly if that is your group's practice. From then on, know the exact tile(s) that complete your hand.

5. Declaring Mahjong

When the drawn or legally claimed tile completes a valid hand, stop play and declare Mahjong. Lay out the hand in logical groups so everyone can verify it against the named pattern.

For an ordinary structure, think in groups: sets (Chows/Pungs/Kongs as allowed) plus the required pair. Your special hands can replace that ordinary structure—Seven Twins, All Pair, runs, Wind/Dragon hands, etc. must match their listed recipe exactly.

Before paying: verify (1) the hand name, (2) concealed/exposed requirement, (3) Fishing/pick-up restriction, and (4) whether your sheet marks it L, H, L×2, etc. Then use your group's established settlement/payment table. I have deliberately not invented a payment table that was not in the uploaded material.

6. Your special-hand system

Your reference sheets classify hands by recipes and values such as L, H, and L×2. Here are the ones most useful to recognize quickly.

Crazy Chows

Your book illustration shows four mixed Chows + a mixed pair. The photographed book page labels it Half Limit (concealed) and Fishing = 200.

Ordinary

Under “one suit with Winds and/or Dragons,” your sheet says: Pungs, 1 pair; 1 Chow is OK.

All Pair

All pairs. Your reference marks this as a Half hand.

Seven Twins

Seven pairs — anything. Your sheet marks it H.

Windy Chow

Chow in each suit + one of each Wind + one Wind paired.

Little Arthur

Chow in each suit + 1 Pung of Winds and/or Dragons + 1 pair of Winds/Dragons.

Bombshell

Chow in each suit + one of each Dragon + one pair of Winds.

Western Command

Any 3 Pungs + one Chow + one pair.

Four Blessings

Pung in each Wind + any pair.

All Winds & Dragons

Pungs of Winds and Dragons + one pair; no suit tiles.

Chop Suey

Chows 1-2-3 in each suit + one of each Wind + one paired.

Chow Mein

Chows 7-8-9 in each suit + one of each Wind + one paired.

Knitting

Pairs in two suits.

Heads and Tails

Four Pungs/Kongs of 1s and 9s + a pair of 1s or 9s.

7. “What do I do right now?” table

SituationQuick answer
I just drew a tile.See whether it improves/completes your target hand; unless you win or declare something, discard one.
Someone discarded something I want.Check whether you can legally use it for the set/hand you are building before touching it.
I have 3 identical tiles and draw the 4th.You may have a Kong. Pause and follow the Kong/replacement procedure your group uses.
I need only one tile.You are Fishing. Check the * / ** restriction for your named hand.
I think I won.Stop. Declare Mahjong. Lay the hand out by groups and identify the exact hand before scoring.
Two people want the same discard.Use your group's established claim-priority rule; do not resolve it from memory of a different Mahjong variant.
Not sure which special hand I'm making.Stay flexible. Do not expose sets unnecessarily; compare your tiles with the photographed reference.

Tonight's simplest play plan

First hand: don't chase an exotic hand unless your opening tiles clearly suggest one. Relearn the draw → assess → discard rhythm. Second hand onward: start watching for the named patterns. When anyone says “Fishing,” pause for two seconds and check the asterisk rule. When anyone says “Mahjong,” verify the recipe before scoring.

This makes the reference useful at the table without turning tonight into a rulebook-reading session.
